title: もう and まだ: the time relations
summary: まだ means a state still holds and a change is expected; もう means the change has already happened. Both are ways of saying now.

blocks.text: Both words are about **now**, seen against a point where things change. **まだ** (still, not yet) says: we are inside a stretch of time that began in the past and is expected to end. **もう** (already) says: the change has happened and we are in the new stretch.

blocks.jp: 宿題はまだしていない。
blocks.en: I haven't done my homework yet.

blocks.text: With a negative, まだ becomes "not yet", but Japanese really says "still not". On its own, **まだまだ** is the modest reply to a compliment: "I still have a long way to go."

blocks.en: No, not yet (I'm still far from good).

blocks.jp: 「宿題をしなさい。」「もうやったよ。」

blocks.en: I'm all right now (no more time needed).

blocks.text: Because もう is also a kind of now, dictionaries sometimes translate it as "now". It carries the nuance that something was different before. A standalone **もう!** is exasperation, like "Enough already!"

items: **まだ**: the present is still inside the old stretch; change is expected later.
**まだ + negative** = not yet; **まだ + positive** = still.
**もう**: the change has already happened; also "now" with a sense of contrast.
**まだまだ**: humble reply; **もう!**: exasperation.

questions.note: もう marks the change as already done.
